course: AP Calculus BC - Limits, Change, Coordinates and Series
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: The full AP Calculus BC sequence: limits and continuity; the derivative from its definition through the power, product, quotient, chain and implicit rules; contextual and analytical applications including related rates, L'Hopital's rule, curve analysis and optimization; integration and accumulation, substitution, parts, partial fractions and improper integrals; differential equations with slope fields, Euler's method and the logistic model; areas, volumes and arc length; parametric, polar and vector-valued functions; and infinite sequences and series through Taylor polynomials, the Lagrange error bound and power series.

concepts.title: Instantaneous Rate as a Limit
concepts.summary: Instantaneous change is reached through average change, so the quotient (f(a + h) - f(a))/h takes the indeterminate form 0/0 as h tends to 0 and must be rewritten or estimated rather than evaluated by substitution.

concepts.title: Limit Notation and Two-Sided Limits
concepts.summary: The statement lim_{x->a} f(x) = L means f(x) can be forced arbitrarily close to L by taking x close to a but not equal to a, and the two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

concepts.title: Limits from Graphs, Tables and Multiple Representations
concepts.summary: A graph, a table and an algebraic form of the same function must agree on the limit wherever it exists, and a hole in the graph alongside an undefined algebraic form is agreement rather than contradiction, because a limit depends on nearby values and not on the value at the point.

concepts.title: The Limit Laws and Direct Substitution
concepts.summary: If the limits of f and g at a exist then the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple or product is the corresponding combination of those limits, the quotient law applies only when the denominator limit is nonzero, and for a function continuous at a direct substitution gives the limit exactly.

concepts.title: Rewriting Quotients That Give 0/0
concepts.summary: If f(x) = g(x) for every x near a except possibly at a, then their limits at a agree, so factoring, multiplying by a conjugate or combining fractions can cancel the factor responsible for the 0/0 form and leave a quotient that substitution evaluates.

topics.topic: Procedure Selection and the Squeeze Theorem

concepts.title: Selecting a Limit Procedure
concepts.summary: Procedures are tried in order of strength - direct substitution, then an algebraic rewrite, then the squeeze theorem or a numerical estimate - and only a law, an identity or a theorem establishes a limit, since a table can always be too coarse to exclude a nearby jump.

concepts.title: The Squeeze Theorem
concepts.summary: If g(x) <= f(x) <= h(x) for all x near a and lim g = lim h = L, then lim f = L at a, and a bounded factor multiplied by a quantity tending to zero therefore has limit zero even when no product law applies.

concepts.title: Removable, Jump and Infinite Discontinuities
concepts.summary: A discontinuity at a is removable when the two-sided limit exists but f(a) is missing or different, a jump when both one-sided limits exist and differ, and infinite when at least one one-sided limit is unbounded.

topics.topic: Continuity at a Point and on an Interval

concepts.title: The Continuity Conditions
concepts.summary: f is continuous at a exactly when f(a) is defined, lim_{x->a} f(x) exists and the two are equal, and f is continuous on a closed interval when it is continuous at every interior point and its one-sided limits at the endpoints equal the endpoint values.

concepts.title: Repairing a Removable Discontinuity
concepts.summary: A discontinuity at a is removable exactly when lim_{x->a} f(x) = L exists, and redefining f(a) = L then makes f continuous at a while leaving every other value unchanged, whereas a jump or an infinite discontinuity admits no such repair.

concepts.title: Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
concepts.summary: lim_{x->a} f(x) = inf means f(x) exceeds any bound once x is close enough to a, and x = a is a vertical asymptote exactly when some one-sided limit at a is infinite, which for a rational function means a zero of the denominator that the numerator does not cancel.

concepts.title: Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
concepts.summary: lim_{x->inf} f(x) = L means f(x) stays arbitrarily close to L for all sufficiently large x, and y = L is then a horizontal asymptote; for a rational function the limit follows from comparing degrees, with a lower-degree numerator forcing the limit to zero.

concepts.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem
concepts.summary: If f is continuous on [a, b] and N lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then some c in (a, b) satisfies f(c) = N, so continuity guarantees that the value is attained while saying nothing about how many such c exist or where they lie.

topics.topic: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change

concepts.title: Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change
concepts.summary: The average rate of change of f on [a, b] is (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a), the slope of the secant through the endpoints, and the instantaneous rate at a is the limit of that quotient as the interval shrinks, which exists only when the left-hand and right-hand quotients agree.

concepts.title: The Derivative at a Point and Its Notation
concepts.summary: f is differentiable at a exactly when lim_{h->0} (f(a + h) - f(a))/h exists, and that value, written f'(a) or dy/dx at x = a, is the slope of the tangent line there, carrying the units of f divided by the units of x.

concepts.title: Estimating a Derivative from Data
concepts.summary: A derivative is estimated from a table by the symmetric quotient (f(a + h) - f(a - h))/(2h), or from a graph by the slope of a secant through two nearby points, and either estimate is limited by the data rather than by the arithmetic.

concepts.title: Differentiability Implies Continuity
concepts.summary: Differentiability at a point implies continuity there, while continuity does not imply differentiability: |x| at 0 has a corner and x^(1/3) at 0 a vertical tangent, and neither has a limiting secant slope.

concepts.title: The Power Rule
concepts.summary: For every constant real exponent n, d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) on every interval where x^n is defined and differentiable, which for negative and fractional exponents restricts the domain to x > 0.

concepts.title: Constant, Sum, Difference and Constant-Multiple Rules
concepts.summary: The derivative of a constant is zero and differentiation is linear, so (c f +- g)' = c f' +- g' wherever both derivatives exist, which is what lets a polynomial be differentiated term by term.

topics.topic: Derivatives of Sine, Cosine, e^x and ln x

concepts.title: The Derivatives of Sine and Cosine
concepts.summary: d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = -sin x for every real x, and the pair cycles with period four through -sin x and -cos x, so the fourth derivative of either function is the function itself.

concepts.title: The Derivatives of e^x and ln x
concepts.summary: d/dx e^x = e^x for every real x because e is the base whose exponential is its own derivative, and d/dx ln x = 1/x for x > 0, with the chain rule extending them to e^(u)u' and u'/u wherever u is nonzero.
prerequisites: The Derivatives of Sine and Cosine

concepts.title: The Product Rule
concepts.summary: If f and g are differentiable at x then (fg)'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x), and the rule is required because the derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives unless one factor is constant.

concepts.title: The Quotient Rule
concepts.summary: If f and g are differentiable at x with g(x) nonzero then (f/g)'(x) = (f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x))/g(x)^2, and the subtraction makes the order of the numerator terms significant.

topics.topic: Derivatives of the Remaining Trigonometric Functions

concepts.title: Tangent, Cotangent, Secant and Cosecant Derivatives
concepts.summary: d/dx tan x = sec^2 x and d/dx sec x = sec x tan x hold where cos x is nonzero, while d/dx cot x = -csc^2 x and d/dx csc x = -csc x cot x hold where sin x is nonzero, so each formula is valid only on the domain of the function it differentiates.

strands.strand: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit and Inverse Functions

units.unit: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit and Inverse Functions

concepts.title: The Chain Rule
concepts.summary: If g is differentiable at x and f is differentiable at g(x), then d/dx f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) g'(x), so the outer derivative is evaluated at the inner function and multiplied by the inner derivative, with one application per layer of composition.

concepts.title: Implicit Differentiation
concepts.summary: If y is defined implicitly by an equation in x and y, differentiating both sides with respect to x while treating y as a differentiable function of x produces an equation linear in dy/dx, provided the tangent at the point is not vertical.

concepts.title: The Inverse Function Derivative Rule
concepts.summary: If f is differentiable and one-to-one near a with f'(a) nonzero, then its inverse is differentiable at b = f(a) with (f^-1)'(b) = 1/f'(a), so slopes at mirrored points are reciprocals and a horizontal tangent in f becomes a vertical tangent in its inverse.

concepts.title: Derivatives of the Inverse Trigonometric Functions
concepts.summary: d/dx arcsin x = 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) and d/dx arccos x = -1/sqrt(1 - x^2) hold on |x| < 1, while d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x^2) and d/dx arccot x = -1/(1 + x^2) hold for every real x, each one following from the inverse rule on a chosen branch.

concepts.title: Choosing a Differentiation Procedure
concepts.summary: The structure of the expression selects the rule - a sum term by term, a product by the product rule, a quotient by the quotient rule, a composition by the chain rule - and an equation that cannot be solved for y is differentiated implicitly instead of after isolating y.

concepts.title: Higher-Order Derivatives and Their Meaning
concepts.summary: The second derivative f'' is the derivative of f', the n-th derivative exists at a only when every lower one exists and is differentiable near a, and f'' measures how the slope itself is changing, which in a motion model is acceleration.

concepts.title: Interpreting a Derivative in Context
concepts.summary: In a context the derivative is the rate of change of the modelled quantity with respect to the independent variable, carrying the units of the output over the units of the input, so its sign gives direction, its magnitude gives how fast, a zero derivative marks a stationary instant rather than necessarily an extremum, and a marginal rate such as marginal cost describes the next unit rather than an average over an interval.

concepts.title: Position, Velocity and Acceleration
concepts.summary: For motion along a line v(t) = s'(t) and a(t) = v'(t), so speed is |v(t)|, a particle speeds up exactly where velocity and acceleration share a sign, and a zero velocity with nonzero acceleration is a momentary stop where the direction reverses.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Related Rate
concepts.summary: A related-rate problem begins with an equation among the quantities, differentiates both sides with respect to time so every derivative becomes a rate, and substitutes the instantaneous values only afterwards, because the relation among the rates must be differentiated before the numbers are fixed.

concepts.title: Solving a Related Rate
concepts.summary: The unknown rate is isolated in the differentiated relation and evaluated at the instant in question, then checked for sign and units, since a length that is decreasing must give a negative rate even when the geometry is described with positive lengths.

concepts.title: Local Linearity and the Tangent Line Approximation
concepts.summary: Near a point of differentiability the tangent line approximates the curve, f(x) is approximately f(a) + f'(a)(x - a), and the approximation is local because its error vanishes faster than |x - a| while the second derivative decides whether the estimate is an over- or underestimate.

concepts.title: L'Hopital's Rule and Its Indeterminate Forms
concepts.summary: If f and g are differentiable near a with g' nonzero there and the quotient has the form 0/0 or inf/inf, then lim f/g = lim f'/g' whenever the latter limit exists or is infinite, whereas the forms 0*inf, inf - inf, 0^0, 1^inf and inf^0 must first be rewritten as a quotient or a logarithm before the rule can apply.

prerequisites: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit and Inverse Functions

concepts.title: The Mean Value Theorem
concepts.summary: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then some c in (a, b) satisfies f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a), so some tangent is parallel to the secant through the endpoints, and both hypotheses are needed since a corner allows no parallel tangent.

concepts.title: Absolute Extrema and the Extreme Value Theorem
concepts.summary: A function continuous on a closed interval attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum there, and the conclusion fails once the interval is open, since 1/x on (0, 1] is unbounded and attains no maximum.

concepts.title: Local Extrema and Critical Points
concepts.summary: A local extremum at an interior point where f is differentiable forces f' = 0 there, so the critical points - zeros of f' and points where f' does not exist - are the only candidates, although a critical point need not be an extremum, as x^3 at 0 shows.
prerequisites: Absolute Extrema and the Extreme Value Theorem

topics.topic: Increase, Decrease and the First Derivative Test

concepts.title: Intervals of Increase and Decrease
concepts.summary: On an interval where f' > 0 the function is increasing and where f' < 0 it is decreasing, and the sign of f' can change only at a zero or a point where it is undefined, so those points alone separate the monotone intervals.

concepts.title: The First Derivative Test
concepts.summary: At a critical point c the function has a local maximum where f' changes from positive to negative, a local minimum where it changes from negative to positive, and neither where the sign of f' does not change.

concepts.title: The Candidates Test
concepts.summary: The absolute extrema of a continuous function on a closed interval occur only at its critical points inside the interval or at the two endpoints, so comparing f at that finite list identifies the global maximum and minimum without any sign analysis.

concepts.title: Concavity and Points of Inflection
concepts.summary: A graph is concave up where f'' > 0 and concave down where f'' < 0, and a point of inflection requires the concavity to change across it, so f'' = 0 alone is insufficient and an inflection can also occur where f'' is undefined.

concepts.title: The Second Derivative Test
concepts.summary: Where f'(c) = 0, a positive f''(c) makes c a local minimum and a negative f''(c) makes it a local maximum, while f''(c) = 0 is inconclusive and returns the question to the first derivative test.

concepts.title: Reading Slopes from the Graph of f
concepts.summary: The graph of f' records the slope of f: positive where f rises, negative where f falls, zero at horizontal tangents, and greatest at the input where f is steepest upwards, so a local extremum of f' marks a change in how fast f is climbing.

concepts.title: Reading f from the Graph of Its Derivative
concepts.summary: The sign of f' gives the intervals where f increases or decreases, its zeros give the critical points and, with its sign changes, the extrema of f, while the increase or decrease of f' itself gives the concavity of f, and f is then determined only up to a vertical translation until one function value is known.
prerequisites: Reading Slopes from the Graph of f

concepts.title: Setting Up an Optimization Problem
concepts.summary: An optimization problem names the objective, uses the constraint to express it as a function of one variable, and records the domain the context permits before differentiating, since a critical point outside the physical domain is not a solution.

concepts.title: Justifying an Optimum
concepts.summary: A candidate optimum is confirmed by the candidates test on a closed domain or, on an open domain, by a sign change of f' or by the second derivative test, because on a closed interval an endpoint can beat every interior critical point.

concepts.title: Horizontal and Vertical Tangents on Implicit Curves
concepts.summary: On an implicitly defined curve dy/dx vanishes where its numerator does, giving a horizontal tangent, and fails to exist where its denominator vanishes with a nonzero numerator, giving a vertical tangent, provided the point satisfies the original equation.

concepts.title: Accumulated Change from a Rate
concepts.summary: If r(t) is the rate at which a quantity changes, the accumulated change on [a, b] is the limit of sums of the form sum r(t_k) dt, which is the area under the graph when r is nonnegative and the net signed area otherwise.

concepts.title: Left, Right and Midpoint Riemann Sums
concepts.summary: A Riemann sum multiplies each subinterval width by the rate sampled at its left endpoint, its right endpoint or its midpoint, and the three agree in the limit although at finite n a left sum underestimates an increasing rate while a right sum overestimates it.

concepts.title: Sigma Notation and the Definite Integral
concepts.summary: Sigma notation writes a sum as sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k, with the closed forms for sum k and sum k^2 used to evaluate a Riemann sum before the limit is taken, and the definite integral is that limit as the widest subinterval tends to zero, existing only when every partition and every sample choice gives the same value.

topics.topic: The Fundamental Theorem and Accumulation Functions

concepts.title: The Accumulation Function and the Fundamental Theorem
concepts.summary: If f is continuous on an interval containing a, then g(x) = int_a^x f(t) dt satisfies g'(x) = f(x) there, so differentiation undoes integration at a variable upper limit, and a differentiable limit u(x) adds the factor u'(x) by the chain rule.

concepts.title: Behaviour of an Accumulation Function
concepts.summary: Because g' = f, an accumulation function increases where f is positive, has a local extremum where f changes sign, and is concave up where f is increasing, so the shape of g is read entirely from the graph of f.
prerequisites: The Accumulation Function and the Fundamental Theorem

concepts.title: Properties of the Definite Integral
concepts.summary: For integrable functions the integral is linear, additive over adjacent intervals, zero on an interval of zero width, and changes sign when its limits are exchanged, which is what allows a region to be split and recombined across subintervals.

concepts.title: The Fundamental Theorem, Part 2
concepts.summary: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F is any antiderivative of f there, then int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), which turns a limit of sums into two evaluations and fails if f is not continuous across the whole interval.

concepts.title: Antiderivatives, the Constant of Integration and Basic Rules
concepts.summary: An antiderivative of f on an interval is a function F with F' = f there, any two of them differ by a constant on that interval so the indefinite integral carries + C, and the power rule holds for every constant n except n = -1, where the antiderivative is ln|x|.

concepts.title: Integration by Substitution
concepts.summary: With u = g(x) and du = g'(x) dx, the chain rule read backwards gives int f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = int f(u) du, so the method applies only when the inner derivative appears as a factor, possibly up to a constant multiple.

concepts.title: Substitution with Changed Limits
concepts.summary: In a definite integral the limits must be converted to u-values when the substitution is made, since x-limits left on a u-antiderivative evaluate the wrong endpoints, and the substitution must be one-to-one on the interval of integration.

topics.topic: Long Division and Completing the Square

concepts.title: Long Division and Completing the Square
concepts.summary: A rational integrand whose numerator degree is at least the denominator degree is rewritten by polynomial division as a polynomial plus a proper fraction, and a quadratic denominator carrying a linear term is completed to (x - h)^2 + k so that it matches an arctangent or a logarithm formula.

concepts.title: Integration by Parts
concepts.summary: Integration by parts restates the product rule as int u dv = uv - int v du, and it is the right choice when the new integral is simpler than the original; applying it twice reduces x^2 e^x, while on e^x sin x it returns the original integral and the equation is solved for it instead.

concepts.title: Linear Partial Fractions
concepts.summary: A proper rational function whose denominator factors into distinct linear factors decomposes into A/(x - r) terms, a repeated factor (x - r)^k contributes one term for each power up to k, and every term then integrates to a logarithm or to a negative power.

concepts.title: Improper Integrals
concepts.summary: An integral over an infinite interval or with an unbounded integrand is defined as a limit of proper integrals at the offending endpoint or interior singularity, converging exactly when that limit is finite, so int_1^inf x^(-p) dx converges for p > 1 and int_0^1 x^(-p) dx converges for p < 1.

concepts.title: Selecting an Integration Technique
concepts.summary: The integrand is inspected before a rule is chosen: a composition carrying its inner derivative suggests substitution, a product of unlike types suggests parts, a proper rational function suggests partial fractions, and a quadratic denominator suggests completing the square.

concepts.title: Writing a Differential Equation from a Context
concepts.summary: A verbal rate statement becomes a differential equation by replacing the rate of change with a derivative and proportionality with a constant multiple, so a population growing at a rate proportional to its size satisfies dP/dt = kP with k carrying the units of inverse time.

concepts.title: Verifying a Solution by Substitution
concepts.summary: A function is a solution of a differential equation on an interval exactly when substituting it and its derivatives into the equation produces an identity for every x in that interval, which is the only accepted verification.

concepts.title: Sketching and Reading a Slope Field
concepts.summary: A slope field plots a segment of slope dy/dx at each sample point, computed from the equation alone, so a solution curve must stay tangent to the segment where it passes, a horizontal segment marks a constant solution, and a curve drawn through the field is consistent with the equation rather than a proof of a formula.

concepts.title: Euler's Method
concepts.summary: Euler's method advances a solution along its tangent line for one step of size h, using y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n), so the approximation improves as h shrinks but drifts from the true curve wherever the solution bends.

concepts.title: Separation of Variables and Particular Solutions
concepts.summary: A separable equation dy/dx = f(x)g(y) is solved by dividing so that every y-term sits with dy and every x-term with dx, integrating both sides, and fixing the single constant with the initial condition, while the division is valid only where g(y) is nonzero, so the constant solutions at the zeros of g must be recorded separately.

concepts.title: Exponential Growth and Decay Models
concepts.summary: The equation dy/dt = ky has the solution y = C e^(kt), growing for positive k and decaying for negative k, and a doubling time or half-life T fixes the constant through k = ln 2 / T with the sign of T matching the direction of change.

concepts.title: The Logistic Model and Its Point of Inflection
concepts.summary: The logistic equation dP/dt = kP(1 - P/K) has carrying capacity K, so a solution starting between 0 and K increases towards K without reaching it in finite time, and its growth rate is greatest at P = K/2, where the solution also changes concavity.

concepts.title: The Average Value of a Function
concepts.summary: The average value of a continuous f on [a, b] is (1/(b - a)) int_a^b f(x) dx, the height of the rectangle whose signed area over the interval equals the integral, and continuity guarantees that f actually attains this value somewhere on [a, b].

concepts.title: Position, Velocity and Acceleration with Integrals
concepts.summary: The integral of velocity over [a, b] is the displacement s(b) - s(a) while the integral of |v| is the distance travelled, so recovering position requires an initial value and reads s(b) = s(a) + int_a^b v(t) dt.

concepts.title: Net Change in an Applied Model
concepts.summary: For any quantity whose rate of change is known, the net change over an interval is the integral of that rate, which is why a tank volume, a population and a bank balance are all handled as net change problems with the units of the rate times the units of time.

concepts.title: Area Between Curves in x and in y
concepts.summary: The area between two curves is int (upper - lower) dx when the region is sliced vertically and int (right - left) dy when it is sliced horizontally, and the correct slicing is the one that keeps a single pair of boundary curves across the whole region.

concepts.title: Regions with More Than Two Intersections
concepts.summary: When the boundary curves meet more than twice, the region is split at every interior intersection and the integral of (upper - lower) is taken piecewise, because which curve lies on top can change from one piece to the next.
prerequisites: Area Between Curves in x and in y

concepts.title: Square and Rectangular Cross Sections
concepts.summary: For a solid whose cross sections perpendicular to an axis are squares on a base of length b(x), the volume is int b(x)^2 dx, and rectangular sections require the second side length as a function of x as well.

concepts.title: Triangular and Semicircular Cross Sections
concepts.summary: Cross sections that are equilateral triangles or semicircles on a base of length b(x) have areas (sqrt 3 / 4) b(x)^2 and (pi / 8) b(x)^2 respectively, so the volume is that area integrated along the axis.

concepts.title: The Disc Method about Either Axis
concepts.summary: Revolving a region that reaches from an axis out to a curve sweeps discs whose radius is the distance to the axis, so the volume is int pi f(x)^2 dx about the x-axis and int pi g(y)^2 dy about the y-axis, provided every cross section is a full disc.

concepts.title: The Washer Method about Either Axis
concepts.summary: When the region does not reach the axis of revolution, each cross section is a washer of area pi (R^2 - r^2), so the volume is the integral of that area along the axis with R and r the distances from the axis to the outer and inner curves.

concepts.title: Arc Length and Distance Travelled
concepts.summary: The length of a curve y = f(x) with continuous derivative from a to b is int_a^b sqrt(1 + f'(x)^2) dx, and it equals the distance travelled only when the motion follows that curve exactly once without reversing direction.

strands.strand: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates and Vector-Valued Functions

units.unit: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates and Vector-Valued Functions

concepts.title: Defining and Differentiating Parametric Equations
concepts.summary: A parametric curve (x(t), y(t)) has slope dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) wherever dx/dt is nonzero, so the tangent is vertical where dx/dt vanishes with dy/dt nonzero and the quotient is undefined where both vanish.

concepts.title: Second Derivatives of Parametric Curves
concepts.summary: The second derivative of a parametric curve is d^2y/dx^2 = (d/dt (dy/dx))/(dx/dt), not the quotient of the second derivatives, because dy/dx is a function of t that must be differentiated with respect to t and then divided by dx/dt.

concepts.title: Arc Length of a Parametric Curve
concepts.summary: The length of a parametric curve traced exactly once on [t1, t2] is int sqrt((dx/dt)^2 + (dy/dt)^2) dt, and the formula requires continuous derivatives and a single traversal, since a retraced arc is counted twice.

concepts.title: Defining and Differentiating Vector-Valued Functions
concepts.summary: A vector-valued function r(t) = <x(t), y(t)> is differentiable exactly when both components are, and r'(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)> is tangent to the path at r(t) whenever it is nonzero.

concepts.title: Integrating Vector-Valued Functions
concepts.summary: A vector-valued function is integrated componentwise, int r(t) dt = <int x dt, int y dt> + C, and the constant of integration is itself a vector because the position is determined only up to a translation.

concepts.title: Motion with Vector-Valued Functions
concepts.summary: For a particle with position vector r(t), velocity is r'(t), acceleration is r''(t) and speed is the magnitude |r'(t)| rather than any component, while displacement over an interval is the integral of the velocity vector.

concepts.title: Polar Coordinates and Differentiation in Polar Form
concepts.summary: A polar curve r = f(theta) has slope dy/dx = (f'(theta) sin theta + f(theta) cos theta)/(f'(theta) cos theta - f(theta) sin theta) wherever that denominator is nonzero, and the curve passes through the pole where f(theta) = 0.

concepts.title: Area of a Polar Region
concepts.summary: The area swept by r = f(theta) from alpha to beta is 1/2 int f(theta)^2 dtheta, valid when the curve is traced exactly once on that interval so that no sector is counted twice.
prerequisites: Polar Coordinates and Differentiation in Polar Form

concepts.title: Area Between Two Polar Curves
concepts.summary: The area between an outer curve r = f(theta) and an inner curve r = g(theta) over a common angular interval is 1/2 int (f^2 - g^2) dtheta, with the interval cut at the angles where the curves meet.

concepts.title: Partial Sums, Convergence and Divergence
concepts.summary: An infinite series converges exactly when its sequence of partial sums has a finite limit, so the sum is defined by that limit rather than by adding infinitely many terms, and a series whose partial sums fail to settle diverges.

concepts.title: Geometric Series and Their Sums
concepts.summary: A geometric series sum a r^n converges to a/(1 - r) exactly when |r| < 1 and diverges for |r| at least 1, which makes it the one family whose sum is available in closed form and therefore the standard comparison target.

concepts.title: The nth-Term Test for Divergence
concepts.summary: If the terms of a series do not tend to zero then the series diverges, but terms tending to zero prove nothing, as the harmonic series shows, so the test can establish divergence only.

concepts.title: The Integral Test
concepts.summary: If f is positive, continuous and decreasing on [N, inf) with a_n = f(n), then the series and the integral of f from N to infinity either both converge or both diverge, and all three hypotheses are needed because a non-decreasing f breaks the rectangle comparison.

concepts.title: The Harmonic Series and the p-Series Test
concepts.summary: The p-series sum 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1 and diverges for p at most 1, so the harmonic series diverges even though its terms tend to zero, and p = 1 is precisely the boundary where the integral test returns a logarithm.

concepts.title: The Direct and Limit Comparison Tests
concepts.summary: If 0 <= a_n <= b_n eventually then convergence of the larger series forces convergence of the smaller and divergence of the smaller forces divergence of the larger, and when only a_n/b_n tends to a finite positive number the two series share their convergence behaviour.

concepts.title: The Alternating Series Test
concepts.summary: An alternating series whose term magnitudes decrease eventually and tend to zero converges, and both conditions are required, since a decreasing sequence with a nonzero limit and a zero limit without decrease both permit divergence.

concepts.title: Absolute and Conditional Convergence
concepts.summary: A series converges absolutely when the series of absolute values converges, which implies convergence of the original, while conditional convergence means the original converges but the absolute version diverges, as with the alternating harmonic series.

concepts.title: The Ratio Test
concepts.summary: For a series of eventually nonzero terms the ratio test gives convergence when lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 and divergence when that limit exceeds 1, while a limit of exactly 1 is inconclusive - the p-series boundary - and the integral or comparison test must decide there.

concepts.title: The Alternating Series Error Bound
concepts.summary: For a convergent alternating series satisfying the alternating series test, the error from truncating after n terms is at most the magnitude of the first omitted term, so the bound is available only while the hypotheses of that test hold.

concepts.title: Taylor Polynomials about a Point
concepts.summary: The n-th Taylor polynomial of f about a is the sum of f^(k)(a)(x - a)^k/k! for k from 0 to n, and it agrees with f in value and in its first n derivatives at a, which is why it is the degree-n polynomial that best fits f near a.

concepts.title: The Lagrange Error Bound
concepts.summary: The error of the n-th Taylor polynomial at x equals f^(n+1)(c)(x - a)^(n+1)/(n+1)! for some c between a and x, so bounding the (n+1)-st derivative on that interval bounds the error, and the bound is useful only where such a bound is available.

concepts.title: Radius and Interval of Convergence
concepts.summary: A power series converges absolutely on the open interval |x - a| < R and diverges outside it, with R found from the ratio test, and the two endpoints must then be tested separately because the radius alone says nothing about them.

concepts.title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series
concepts.summary: A function with derivatives of every order at a has the Taylor series formed from those derivatives, and the series equals the function on its interval of convergence only when the remainder tends to zero there; the Maclaurin series is the case a = 0.

concepts.title: Representing Functions as Power Series
concepts.summary: A known series such as 1/(1 - x) equal to the sum of x^n for |x| < 1 may be differentiated, integrated or composed term by term inside its interval of convergence, which produces new representations without new coefficients being computed.

prerequisites: Parametric Equations, Polar Coordinates and Vector-Valued Functions
